summary: AEAD algorithms protect both the secrecy and the integrity of data. As research produces algorithms with extra properties, this informational RFC provides definitions for those properties so that people comparing and choosing algorithms use terms the same way.

eli5.summary: A sealed envelope should hide the letter and show if anyone changed it. This gives names for the extra special features some sealed envelopes have.

subtitle: A dictionary of special properties that sealed algorithms can have

tldr.problem: As cryptography research advances, AEAD algorithms gain new special properties beyond basic secrecy and integrity. Different papers use different names for the same property, causing confusion when choosing an algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms for 18 additional properties of AEAD algorithms: 10 security properties (like full commitment, key commitment, multi-user security) and 8 implementation properties (like parallelizable, lightweight, streamable).
tldr.outcome: Application designers and protocol authors now have a common vocabulary to specify which extra properties they need from an AEAD algorithm, and algorithm designers can clearly state which properties they provide.

today: RFC 9771 is an informational RFC published by the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) of the IRTF. It provides definitions that protocol and algorithm designers are encouraged to use when specifying AEAD requirements and properties. The document remains the authoritative reference for consistent AEAD terminology.

sections.title: The Need for a Common Language
sections.content:
An AEAD algorithm is a cipher that provides both confidentiality (secrecy of data) and integrity (detection of tampering) at the same time. Examples include AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, and Ascon. These algorithms are mandatory in TLS 1.3, IPsec, and QUIC.

Beyond the basic guarantees of confidentiality and integrity, research has discovered many additional properties that some AEAD algorithms possess: the ability to detect when two different messages encrypt to the same ciphertext (commitment), resistance to nonce reuse, security against quantum computers, and the ability to run on tiny embedded devices.

The problem is that different research papers use different names for the same property, and some properties exist only as folklore without formal definitions. This document standardizes the terminology so that when an RFC says "we need an AEAD algorithm with full commitment," everyone knows what that means.
sections.eli5: Scientists discovered that sealed envelopes can have extra talents, but they kept calling them by different names. This document gives each talent an official name.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
Beyond basic secrecy and integrity, AEAD algorithms can have additional security properties. Full Commitment means it is hard to find two different sets of key, nonce, associated data, and plaintext that encrypt to the same ciphertext; in other words, the ciphertext commits to all its inputs. This is useful for message franking (proving to a social media platform that a message contains abuse).

Key Commitment means it is hard to find two different keys that produce the same ciphertext for the same nonce and plaintext. This helps in password-based encryption and key rotation, where you need to be sure that a ciphertext came from a specific key.

Nonce Misuse Resilience and Resistance both allow some security even if the same nonce is reused, which should never happen but sometimes does due to bugs. Resilience means messages with fresh nonces stay secure. Resistance means all non-repeated messages stay secure. AES-GCM-SIV has full resistance.

Blockwise Security means the algorithm works even if an attacker can change the plaintext after seeing the ciphertext being generated; this is important for streaming.

Multi-user Security means that as you add more users, the security degradation is not as severe as it would be with a naive algorithm.

Quantum Security means the algorithm is secure against quantum computers. Most symmetric algorithms (including AES and ChaCha20) are post-quantum in the Q1 model (where the attacker has quantum computers but uses the encryption oracle classically). The Q2 model (quantum superposition access) is much harder and applies to very few algorithms.
sections.eli5: A really secure envelope proves you packed it yourself, survives even if you accidentally reuse a seal, and works with a quantum computer. These are superpowers.

sections.title: Implementation Properties
sections.content:
Some AEAD algorithms are designed for specific computing environments. Lightweight algorithms run efficiently on tiny devices like IoT sensors or smart cards. Hardware Efficient algorithms are optimized for specific hardware like CPUs with AES instructions.

Parallelizable algorithms can split plaintext into chunks and encrypt them in parallel, useful for fast encryption on multicore processors. Single Pass means encryption reads the data once from beginning to end, without needing multiple passes. Streamable (or Online) means the algorithm can write out ciphertext as data comes in, using constant memory, useful for real-time streaming.

Setup-Free means using a new key incurs minimal overhead; algorithms that require precomputation of a key schedule are not setup-free. Inverse-Free means the algorithm does not need to call the inverse of its underlying primitive (like AES-decrypt), which can be simpler or faster on some hardware.

Static Associated Data Efficient means the algorithm can precompute values for data that is repeatedly authenticated (like a header in many messages), so the header does not slow things down after the first message.
sections.eli5: Some envelopes seal fast on your phone, some work on your smartwatch, some let you seal many at once in parallel, and some let you seal one letter as pages arrive instead of waiting for the whole thing.

sections.title: Using This Taxonomy
sections.content:
The RFC is intended for two use cases. First, when an RFC defines a new AEAD algorithm, it should list which properties from this document the algorithm provides. Second, when an RFC defines a protocol that uses AEAD, it should specify which properties are required.

Not all properties are equally important. Basic security (confidentiality, integrity, authenticated encryption) is required by all algorithms. Additional properties should only be required if the application genuinely needs them, because they often come with trade-offs in performance, implementation complexity, or compatibility.

For example, if your protocol needs to detect forged ciphertexts in real-time streaming, you might require RUP Integrity (Release of Unverified Plaintext integrity). If you need to work with tiny embedded devices, you might require Lightweight. The taxonomy helps you express what you need precisely.

The document emphasizes that claimed properties must undergo formal security analysis in a recognized security model. Using a security notion not referenced in the RFC is allowed but must be clearly documented.
sections.eli5: If you need a sealed envelope that works on a smartwatch, say so. If you need one that proves you packed it, say so. The salesman now knows which envelopes to offer.
